events.description: In 2008, Chinese dairy company Sanlu was found to have adulterated infant formula with melamine, an industrial chemical added to fake higher protein readings — sickening 300,000 babies, killing six, and becoming the defining symbol of a regulatory system overwhelmed by the speed of the boom.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Melamine was added specifically to fool nitrogen-based protein tests: the chemical is nitrogen-rich and mimics protein in standard quality-control checks, meaning the fraud was invisible to the tests companies were running. More than 54,000 infants were hospitalized with kidney stones or kidney damage. The scandal engulfed not just Sanlu but dozens of other dairy brands and triggered a global wave of product recalls — Chinese dairy exports were banned in multiple countries, and the Chinese government ultimately paid out hundreds of millions of dollars in compensation.

events.label: The Bird's Nest and the New Beijing
events.description: The Beijing National Stadium — universally nicknamed the Bird's Nest for its interlocking steel lattice — was built in four years and holds 80,000 people; it was the centerpiece of the Olympic opening ceremony that announced China's arrival to the world.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The stadium covers 204,000 square meters (about 50 acres) and broke ground in December 2003, with construction officially starting in March 2004 and finishing just in time in June 2008. It sits in the Olympic Green in Chaoyang district, the same park corridor that holds the Water Cube aquatics center — together they became the two most-photographed buildings of the decade.

events.label: The Global Financial Crisis Hits
events.description: When the American mortgage market collapsed in September 2008 and cascaded into a global crash, Chinese exports fell roughly 20 percent, tens of thousands of factories closed, and an estimated 20 million migrant workers lost their jobs almost overnight.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: China's economic growth, which had been running above 10 percent, slid toward 6 percent by late 2008 — terrifying for a government whose legitimacy rested on steady prosperity. The speed of the reversal was unlike anything since 1989: factory orders dried up faster than workers could be retrained or redeployed, and the rural towns those migrants returned to had not planned to absorb them.

events.label: The Four-Trillion-Yuan Stimulus
events.description: On November 9, 2008, China's State Council announced a four-trillion-yuan (roughly $586 billion) stimulus package — one of the largest fiscal interventions in history relative to GDP — channeled almost entirely into infrastructure, construction, and lending through local-government vehicles.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The plan worked in the short run: growth rebounded from near 6 percent back to over 10 percent by mid-2009. But critics trace the surge in Chinese local-government and state-enterprise debt directly to this moment; the World Bank recommended similar public-works approaches to the US and EU, but both chose quantitative easing instead. The stimulus essentially traded a short-term jobs crisis for a long-term debt mountain.

events.label: The 2009 Export Collapse
events.description: In 2009 Chinese exports dropped roughly 20 percent as global demand evaporated — the steepest fall since the reform era began — forcing Beijing to pivot from an export-led growth model toward debt-financed domestic investment.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The collapse was structural, not just cyclical: the Western consumers who had powered China's factory boom were now deleveraging and would never return to pre-crisis spending rates. That reality made the four-trillion-yuan stimulus not just a rescue measure but a permanent reorientation — from making things for the world to building things for China, paid for with borrowed money.

events.label: The Jasmine Scare
events.description: In February 2011, anonymous online posts called on Chinese citizens to gather at specific street corners for Arab-Spring-style "Jasmine" demonstrations — almost nobody showed up, but the government deployed massive police forces anyway and detained dozens of dissidents preemptively.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The calls for protests spread across over a dozen cities starting February 20, 2011, closely timed to the fall of authoritarian governments in Tunisia and Egypt. The disproportion of the crackdown relative to the actual turnout was itself revealing: the government even censored the word "jasmine" on search engines, scrubbing a flower from the internet because it had become a symbol. The episode showed that Beijing was watching the Arab Spring with something close to terror, not confidence.

events.label: The Detention of Ai Weiwei
events.description: Ai Weiwei, a celebrated contemporary artist and architect who had helped design the Bird's Nest, spent years documenting the names of children killed in collapsed Sichuan schools — then in April 2011 was arrested at Beijing airport and held for 81 days without charge.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ai grew up in China's remote northwest, where his father (the poet Ai Qing) had been exiled during the Anti-Rightist Campaign — giving him a family-level memory of state punishment that shaped his later activism. His arrest was officially for "economic crimes," but followed directly from his investigation of the Sichuan schools corruption scandal. He was released without trial after international pressure, then placed under various forms of surveillance and travel restriction for years.

events.label: The Wenzhou High-Speed Rail Crash
events.description: On July 23, 2011, a high-speed train rear-ended a stalled train on a viaduct near Wenzhou, killing 40 people and injuring at least 192 — and then authorities made it far worse by ordering a wrecked carriage buried while rescuers were still searching for survivors.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The crash was caused by a combination of signal-design defects and poor management — in other words, the very systems meant to make the high-speed network safe had been built too fast and without adequate quality control. Outrage over the burial order spread on Weibo before censors could contain it, turning a railway accident into a national referendum on whether officials cared about the people they were supposed to serve. One infant, Xiang Weiyi, was pulled alive from the wreckage hours after authorities declared the rescue over — a fact that made the premature burial order even harder to forgive.

events.label: The Weibo Moment
events.description: Weibo, a Twitter-like microblog launched in August 2009, gave China its first real semi-public national square — a place where scandals, disasters, and official lies could spread faster than censors could kill them.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Weibo grew to over 582 million monthly active users at its peak, making it one of the largest social media platforms on earth. The platform's open architecture meant viral posts could reach millions in hours, outrunning the state's slow-moving propaganda apparatus — which is precisely why authorities eventually invested heavily in real-time censorship infrastructure and steered traffic toward more controllable apps like WeChat.

events.label: Ghost Cities and the Property Engine
events.description: Debt-fueled construction through the 2010s produced vast newly built districts with almost no residents — "ghost cities" built not because anyone needed to live there, but because building kept the growth numbers up and generated tax revenue for local governments.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The phenomenon was first reported as early as 2009, before the wave peaked. Notably, many developments initially condemned as permanent ghost cities have since filled in and become functioning urban centers — the phenomenon was partly a timing artifact of China's rapid internal migration, not pure overbuilding. The property sector eventually grew to account for roughly a quarter of China's total economic activity, making it both the country's biggest growth engine and its deepest structural vulnerability.

events.label: Bo Xilai and the Chongqing Model
events.description: Bo Xilai, the Communist Party chief of the giant megacity of Chongqing (population: roughly 30 million), built a national profile from 2007 to 2012 through a nostalgia-fueled Maoist "red culture" campaign and a brutal crackdown on organized crime — openly positioning himself for the top leadership in a system where openly positioning yourself is forbidden.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Bo came from the very top of China's political aristocracy: his father, Bo Yibo, was a founding revolutionary elder and a member of the "Eight Immortals" who shaped the post-Mao era. Before Chongqing, Bo served as Mayor of Dalian, Governor of Liaoning, and Minister of Commerce — a career path engineered for the summit. His Chongqing anti-mafia drive, called "Strike Black," was later found to have used torture and fabricated evidence, targeting rivals as much as criminals.

events.label: The Wang Lijun Incident
events.description: On February 6, 2012, Wang Lijun — Bo Xilai's police chief and chief enforcer of the Chongqing crime crackdown — walked into the US consulate in Chengdu and spent over 30 hours there, handing over evidence that Bo's wife, Gu Kailai, had poisoned British businessman Neil Heywood.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Wang had apparently fallen out with Bo after confronting him with evidence of Gu's role in the murder, and feared Bo would have him killed. The Chinese government's initial cover story was that Wang had gone to the consulate for "vacation-style medical treatment" — a phrase so absurd it became a dark joke. Wang eventually left the consulate voluntarily and was taken directly to Beijing by state security agents; he was later sentenced to 15 years in prison for defection and bending the law.

events.label: The Fall of Bo Xilai
events.description: By September 2013, Bo Xilai had been expelled from the Communist Party, stripped of all offices, tried on charges of bribery, embezzlement, and abuse of power, and sentenced to life in prison — the most spectacular elite downfall in China since the Gang of Four in 1976.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Bo's wife, Gu Kailai, was separately convicted of Neil Heywood's murder and received a suspended death sentence (meaning life imprisonment in practice). The trial itself was tightly managed, but Bo's combative courtroom performance — denying charges, retracting his confession, challenging witnesses — was unusual enough that the proceedings were partially live-blogged by Chinese state media, an unprecedented move apparently designed to demonstrate procedural legitimacy. The affair cleared the field for Xi Jinping and also gave the new leadership a powerful template for using anti-corruption prosecutions against political rivals.

events.label: The 18th Party Congress
events.description: The 18th National Congress of the Communist Party, held November 8–14, 2012, formally installed Xi Jinping as party General Secretary and handed him command of the military — completing a once-a-decade leadership handover in a system with no elections, where succession is decided entirely by elite bargaining behind closed doors.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The congress had 2,268 delegates, but real decisions had been made in the months before by the outgoing Standing Committee. Xi was broadly understood at the time as a safe, dull consensus choice — a "compromise candidate" whose main qualification was that he had not made dangerous enemies. Within two years that reading would look like the biggest political miscalculation in modern Chinese history, as Xi moved to consolidate personal power on a scale not seen since Mao.

events.label: Tigers and Flies
events.description: Xi's phrase 'hunting both tigers and flies' — senior officials and petty bureaucrats alike — became the campaign's defining slogan, and its biggest tiger was Zhou Yongkang, the retired security czar and Politburo Standing Committee member prosecuted in 2014, the most senior figure ever jailed in PRC history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Zhou Yongkang had overseen China's vast domestic security apparatus, including the police, courts, and secret services, and his network of allies inside those institutions made him genuinely dangerous to Xi's consolidation of power. He was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2015. The generals caught in the same sweep included Xu Caihou and Guo Boxiong, the two most senior officers in the People's Liberation Army — both former vice chairmen of the Central Military Commission — accused of selling promotions for cash.

events.label: The Chinese Dream
events.description: The 'Chinese Dream' — Xi's signature political concept, formally the 'great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation' — debuted in November 2012 when Xi toured a national-history exhibit titled 'The Road to National Rejuvenation' days after becoming party leader.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The concept set two concrete centenary targets: a 'moderately prosperous society' by 2021, the party's 100th anniversary, and a 'fully developed nation' by 2049, the PRC's centenary. Unlike the Maoist slogans it superficially resembles, the Chinese Dream was explicitly personal and consumerist in its early framing — official messaging emphasized individual prosperity and family comfort — before gradually shifting toward national power and international standing as Xi's tenure lengthened.

events.label: Document No. 9
events.description: Document No. 9 (officially the 'Communiqué on the Current State of the Ideological Sphere') was a classified 2013 directive circulated inside the party listing seven dangerous 'false ideological trends' to be suppressed, from constitutional democracy to an independent press.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The document was leaked to the New York Times in 2013, making its contents public despite never being officially released. Its seventh prohibited topic, 'historical nihilism,' was a direct instruction to prevent honest public discussion of the Great Leap Forward, the Cultural Revolution, and Tiananmen — framing party self-criticism as a foreign-inspired threat. The directive effectively ended the limited tolerance for political debate that had briefly flourished on Weibo between roughly 2009 and 2012.

events.label: The 709 Lawyers Crackdown
events.description: On July 9, 2015 — the '709' date that gave the crackdown its name — police simultaneously detained hundreds of human-rights lawyers and legal activists across China, dismantling the community that had spent a decade trying to use the party's own legal system to defend citizens.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: More than 300 lawyers and activists were eventually detained, questioned, or placed under surveillance. Several of those arrested — including Wang Yu, who had taken on sensitive cases involving Falun Gong practitioners and Uyghurs — were held incommunicado for months and later appeared in televised 'confessions' that rights groups condemned as coerced. The crackdown marked the effective end of the 'rights defense' (weiquan) movement, which had been one of the only organized civil-society forces operating inside China.

events.label: The End of the One-Child Policy
events.description: China replaced the one-child policy with a two-child limit in October 2015 (effective January 2016), not as a liberalizing reform but as a demographic emergency measure — the working-age population had already begun to shrink.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The fertility rate by 2015 had fallen to roughly 1.5–1.6 births per woman, well below the 2.1 replacement level, partly because of the policy and partly because of rising urban living costs. Even after the two-child limit was lifted, birth rates continued to fall — couples who had grown up as only children often chose to remain childless or have one child regardless of official permission. China would further loosen the rule to three children in 2021, then drop all birth limits entirely, but the demographic trajectory barely shifted.

events.label: Xi Named the Core
events.description: In October 2016 the party's Central Committee officially designated Xi Jinping the 'core' (核心, héxīn) of the party's leadership — a status his predecessor Hu Jintao was deliberately never given and that signals a qualitatively different concentration of authority.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The 'core' designation had last been applied to Jiang Zemin, who held it from 1989 onward, and before him to Deng Xiaoping and Mao. Hu Jintao's deliberate exclusion from the title was itself a signal of the collective-leadership era: no single figure was supposed to be indispensable. Restoring it to Xi formalized what had become functionally obvious — that the other six members of the Politburo Standing Committee were no longer peers managing a consensus but subordinates executing his decisions.

events.label: The PLA Overhaul
events.description: Xi restructured the military into joint theater commands, purged its top brass, and reoriented it from a land army toward power projection at sea and in space.

events.label: The Targeted Poverty Campaign
events.description: Xi Jinping's 'Targeted Poverty Alleviation' campaign, launched in 2013, deployed government officials village-by-village to register and assist the rural poor, and in 2020 Beijing declared absolute poverty — as defined by the World Bank threshold — eliminated in China.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The World Bank figure most often cited is that China lifted roughly 800 million people out of extreme poverty over the full reform era from 1978 to 2020 — the largest poverty reduction in human history by any measure. The 'targeted' approach meant individual household registration and personalized intervention, not blanket cash transfers, which made it administratively intensive. Serious economists note that the outcome depends heavily on where the poverty line is set and how much weight to give different phases of reform — the rural land reforms of the 1980s versus the export boom versus the 2013–2020 campaign — but the broad direction of the data is not disputed.

events.label: Made in China 2025
events.description: Signed in 2015, Made in China 2025 was an explicit industrial policy to shift China from cheap-labor assembly into high-tech dominance in ten sectors — including chips, robotics, electric vehicles, and aerospace.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The plan targeted 70% domestic content in high-tech industries by 2025 and set specific market-share goals for Chinese companies both at home and globally. It became a lightning rod in the 2018 US-China trade war — American officials cited it as proof of unfair state-directed competition — and Beijing quietly stopped using the name in official communications after 2019, even as the underlying policy continued. The plan was modeled partly on Germany's 'Industrie 4.0' strategy, which China's planners had studied closely.

events.label: The Platform Economy
events.description: Through the 2010s, Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu, and a wave of startups built a platform economy that for a decade was the most dynamic, globally competitive part of Chinese life — before Beijing turned the regulatory screws.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: At its peak around 2020, Alibaba alone was worth more than $800 billion, and Ant Group — its financial arm — was on track for what would have been the world's largest IPO. The sector's freedom was real but always conditional: companies operated with an implicit license that could be revoked, and it was. Jack Ma's public criticism of Chinese banking regulators in October 2020 triggered a campaign that wiped hundreds of billions off the sector's value within months and made him largely disappear from public life.

events.label: The Cashless Leap
events.description: Between roughly 2014 and 2019, China skipped the credit-card era almost entirely, going from cash to QR-code smartphone payments via two super-apps — Alipay and WeChat Pay — faster than any large economy in history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: China had low credit-card penetration in 2010 partly because state banks were slow to issue them, which left a gap that mobile apps filled almost overnight. By 2019, mobile payments in China totaled roughly $49 trillion annually — more than the entire U.S. economy. The QR code itself, invented in Japan in 1994, became the unlikely backbone of the world's most advanced payment system because it required no special terminal hardware, letting even street vendors join instantly.

events.label: The Surveillance State
events.description: By the late 2010s China had built the world's most sophisticated mass-surveillance network — over 700 million cameras by 2023, facial recognition deployed at transit hubs and city streets, and big-data systems that could flag individuals in real time.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: China's surveillance build-out was partly enabled by homegrown AI companies like Hikvision and Dahua, which became the world's largest manufacturers of surveillance cameras and supplied systems to dozens of other governments. In some pilot cities, facial recognition was used to publicly shame jaywalkers by displaying their faces on digital billboards. The system's data feeds are increasingly integrated with AI, allowing police to predict and pre-empt protests rather than just respond to them after the fact.

events.label: The Social Credit System
events.description: China's 'social credit system' was not the unified citizen score of Western imagination but a real and expanding set of blacklists that could ban people from flights, trains, and schools — enforced with minimal due process.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The system actually operates through dozens of separate databases run by different agencies and municipalities, which is why the dystopian 'one score' image never quite matched reality — though that fragmentation made it harder, not easier, for individuals to challenge or understand why they were blacklisted. The corporate version of the system, which rates businesses on regulatory compliance, is actually older and more developed than the individual version. By 2019, the flight and train blacklists had collectively blocked people from purchasing tickets tens of millions of times.

events.label: The Chang'e Lunar Program
events.description: China's Chang'e lunar program methodically advanced from orbit to landing to far-side landing: in January 2019, Chang'e 4 became the first spacecraft ever to touch down on the Moon's far side, a hemisphere no mission had ever reached.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The far side never faces Earth, which means radio communication requires a relay satellite — China first placed the Queqiao satellite in a special orbital position before Chang'e 4 could even attempt the landing. The rover, named Yutu-2 (Jade Rabbit 2), found evidence of a deep mantle material exposed by an ancient asteroid impact, data not obtainable from the near side. Chang'e 5 followed in 2020 and returned the first lunar samples to Earth since the Soviet Luna 24 mission in 1976.

events.label: The Belt and Road and Its Critics
events.description: Belt and Road loans fueled real infrastructure across Asia, Africa, and Latin America but also generated serious debt problems — and a Western narrative of deliberate 'debt-trap diplomacy' that careful research found largely overstated.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The 'debt-trap' framing became dominant in Western policy circles around 2017–2018, but researchers at Johns Hopkins and elsewhere found that China actually renegotiated or wrote off dozens of loans rather than seizing assets. The more accurate picture is chaotic lending by multiple Chinese state banks with little coordination, not a unified strategic masterplan. That said, Belt and Road did entrench Chinese contractors: most agreements required Chinese firms and Chinese labor, limiting local economic spillover.

events.label: The Hambantota Port Lease
events.description: In 2017, Sri Lanka signed over a 99-year lease on the Chinese-built Hambantota port after the country couldn't service its loans, making the port the global symbol of Belt and Road risk — and of the contested 'debt-trap' debate.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The port was a pet project of Sri Lankan president Mahinda Rajapaksa, not something China pushed on an unwilling government; his own family's political interests in the region partly drove the original decision to build it. Even after the lease, China Merchants Port Holdings — the operator — struggled to make Hambantota commercially viable, since most Sri Lankan trade flows through Colombo to the north. The lease does grant China operational control near a strategically sensitive position in the Indian Ocean, which is why India and the U.S. watched it closely regardless of whether a 'trap' was intended.

events.label: The Umbrella Movement
events.description: A 79-day sit-in occupation of central Hong Kong in 2014, where protesters deployed umbrellas against police pepper spray while demanding genuine universal suffrage for the city's chief executive.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The protests ran from late September to mid-December 2014, paralyzing key commercial districts for over two months. Despite the scale, Beijing made zero concessions — but the movement radicalized a generation of Hong Kong activists who went on to lead the far larger 2019 uprising. The umbrella became the enduring symbol not of victory but of a city that had tried peaceful means and been ignored.

events.label: The Causeway Bay Booksellers
events.description: Five staff of the Causeway Bay bookshop — which sold gossipy, often salacious titles about China's leaders that were banned on the mainland — vanished between October and December 2015, reappearing in mainland custody by early 2016.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: At least two of the five disappeared from mainland China itself, one from Thailand — but the most alarming case was a man who vanished from inside Hong Kong and was later revealed to be in Shenzhen without the travel documents needed to cross the border legally, suggesting he was taken across by mainland agents. One of the five, Swedish citizen Gui Minhai, has been held the longest and repeatedly re-sentenced; as of the mid-2020s he remained in Chinese custody despite international pressure.

events.label: The Hong Kong Exodus
events.description: After the 2020 National Security Law, a wave of Hong Kong residents — particularly professionals, journalists, and activists — emigrated, many using a British National (Overseas) visa scheme created specifically in response to the law.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The UK's BN(O) visa scheme, relaunched in 2021, allowed around three million eligible Hong Kongers and their close family members a path to British residency and eventual citizenship. Estimates suggest over 100,000 people left for Britain alone in the first two years. The emigration hollowed out much of the city's independent civil society, legal profession, and English-language press — losses that accelerated the very transformation the law had been designed to achieve.

events.label: Tsai Ing-wen and the Taiwan Pivot
events.description: Tsai Ing-wen, a legal scholar and member of the independence-leaning Democratic Progressive Party, became Taiwan's first female president in 2016 — a result that effectively ended the warmer cross-strait period that had prevailed under her predecessor.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Tsai served two full terms until 2024 and won re-election in 2020 with the largest popular-vote total in Taiwan's democratic history, widely interpreted as a direct response to events in Hong Kong. She consistently refused to endorse the '1992 Consensus' framework that Beijing demanded as the basis for dialogue, and her tenure coincided with a sharp escalation in Chinese military activity around the island.

events.label: The Sunflower Movement
events.description: In March 2014, Taiwanese students and civic groups occupied the legislature in Taipei to block a services trade agreement with Beijing that critics feared would make Taiwan's economy dangerously dependent on the mainland.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The occupation lasted 24 days, from March 18 to April 10, 2014 — the protesters physically inside the legislature chamber itself, which was unprecedented in Taiwan's history. The agreement they opposed (the Cross-Strait Service Trade Agreement) was never ratified, a direct result of the protest's pressure. The movement permanently shifted Taiwan's political center of gravity against integration and directly boosted the DPP, the party that won the presidency two years later.

events.label: The Ma-Xi Summit
events.description: The first meeting of leaders from the two sides since 1949, in Singapore in 2015, marked the high-water mark of cross-strait engagement before the freeze.

events.label: Military Pressure on Taiwan
events.description: From around 2016 onward, and dramatically accelerating after 2020, the People's Liberation Army began routinely crossing the median line of the Taiwan Strait with warplanes and staging large-scale naval exercises explicitly rehearsing a blockade or invasion.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: PLA aircraft incursions into Taiwan's Air Defense Identification Zone (ADIZ) went from occasional to near-daily by 2020–2021, with single-day records repeatedly broken. The US responded by deepening arms sales and, eventually, unofficial signals of security commitment. The escalation created a situation with no clear de-escalation mechanism — each Chinese exercise prompted US shows of support, which Beijing cited as justification for the next exercise.

events.label: Huawei and the Meng Wanzhou Affair
events.description: In December 2018, Canadian authorities arrested Meng Wanzhou — CFO of Huawei and daughter of its founder Ren Zhengfei — at a Vancouver airport on a US extradition request alleging she had lied to banks about Huawei's dealings with Iran, violating US sanctions. China responded within days by detaining two Canadian citizens, Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor, in conditions widely seen as diplomatic hostage-taking.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Meng was held under house arrest in her Vancouver mansion for almost three years, wearing an ankle monitor, before reaching a deferred prosecution agreement with the US Justice Department in September 2021 — the same day Kovrig and Spavor were released and flown home. The parallel timing made the swap explicit even if both governments denied it. The affair accelerated multiple countries' decisions to exclude Huawei from their 5G networks, costing the company tens of billions in potential contracts.

events.label: The Chip War
events.description: The deeper and more lasting front of the US–China rivalry was semiconductors: from 2019 onward the US progressively barred China from buying the most advanced chips and, more crucially, the Dutch lithography machines and American software without which no one can make them — an attempt to freeze China a generation behind at the one technology that powers everything else.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The key chokepoint was EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography machines made by the Dutch firm ASML — without them, no chip factory on earth can manufacture the most advanced processors. The US persuaded the Netherlands to block ASML exports to China in 2019 and 2023. The 2022 US CHIPS Act simultaneously offered $52 billion in subsidies to rebuild domestic semiconductor manufacturing. The export controls covered not just chips but the specialized software (EDA tools) used to design them, meaning China struggled to design its way around the hardware ban.

events.label: Wolf-Warrior Diplomacy
events.description: Around 2019 China's diplomats abandoned the patient, low-profile soft-power approach of earlier decades for a combative nationalist style nicknamed 'wolf-warrior diplomacy' after a hit Chinese action-film franchise — publicly hectoring host countries, amplifying conspiracy theories, and turning press conferences into confrontations.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The name comes from the Wolf Warrior films (2015 and 2017) — Chinese action blockbusters whose tagline was 'Anyone who offends China, no matter how remote, must be exterminated.' Spokesperson Zhao Lijian became the face of the style, most notoriously posting a fabricated image on Twitter in 2020 suggesting Australian soldiers had murdered an Afghan child. The approach backfired strategically: opinion polling across wealthy democracies showed sharp drops in favorable views of China in 2020–2021, accelerating the very anti-China alignment it was supposedly resisting.

events.label: The South China Sea Ruling
events.description: In 2016 an international arbitral tribunal convened under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea ruled almost entirely against China's sweeping South China Sea claims — and Beijing's response was to ignore the ruling entirely, calling the tribunal illegitimate, and press on with military construction on its artificial islands.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The case was brought by the Philippines, and the tribunal found that China's 'nine-dash line' — the historic boundary claim covering roughly 90% of the South China Sea — had no legal basis under international maritime law. China refused to participate in the proceedings and declared the result 'null and void.' The ruling was the most complete legal rejection of a major power's territorial claim in modern international law, yet had zero enforcement mechanism. No other claimant state has since brought a similar case, partly fearing China's reaction.

events.label: The Galwan Valley Clash
events.description: In June 2020, Indian and Chinese troops fought a savage hand-to-hand battle without firearms — rocks, clubs, and bare fists in freezing Himalayan terrain — in the Galwan Valley, killing at least 20 Indian soldiers and an unacknowledged but significant number of Chinese troops, the worst India–China violence since the 1962 border war.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Both sides' troops had followed long-standing protocols banning firearms in the disputed zone — so the soldiers used rocks, studded clubs, and improvised weapons, fighting in the dark along a glacial river at 14,000 feet (4,270 meters). China did not officially acknowledge any deaths for months; Indian media later reported at least 45 Chinese casualties. The clash was the direct trigger for India banning 59 Chinese apps including TikTok and significantly expanding its Quad engagement — converting what had been an economically cautious India into an active American strategic partner.

events.label: The Quad and AUKUS
events.description: The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue — the US, Japan, India, and Australia — was revived in 2017 and upgraded to leader-level summits in 2021; separately, the AUKUS pact signed the same year committed the US and UK to helping Australia acquire nuclear-powered submarines, building the hard-power architecture of Indo-Pacific pushback against China.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Quad had originally been formed after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami for disaster relief coordination, then quietly shelved after China protested; its revival for security purposes was itself a signal of how much had changed. The AUKUS announcement blindsided France, which had a $66 billion conventional submarine contract with Australia that was instantly cancelled — producing the sharpest transatlantic diplomatic row in years. Australia's first nuclear-powered submarine is not expected to be operational until the early 2030s at the earliest.

events.label: Decoupling and De-Risking
events.description: Beginning around 2018, the word 'decoupling' entered the policy vocabulary to describe the deliberate partial unwinding of US–China economic integration — tariffs, investment bans, export controls, and supply-chain restructuring that together tried to reduce dependence on a strategic rival, later softened to the blander term 'de-risking.'

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The US Foreign Investment Risk Review Modernization Act (FIRRMA, 2018) expanded CFIUS screening of Chinese investment in American companies to cover minority stakes and technology transfers, not just full acquisitions. The 'friend-shoring' concept that followed — moving supply chains to politically allied countries — pushed manufacturing toward Vietnam, India, and Mexico. Despite years of decoupling rhetoric, US–China trade hit record highs in 2022, illustrating how deeply intertwined the two economies remained even as governments tried to separate them.

events.label: The Death of Li Wenliang
events.description: Wuhan ophthalmologist Li Wenliang sent a private WeChat warning to colleagues about a SARS-like illness in December 2019, was summoned by police and forced to sign a statement calling it a false rumor, then caught the virus from a patient and died on February 7, 2020.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Li was only 33 years old when he died. Before his death he gave a final interview from his hospital bed in which he said he hoped recovered patients could return to normal life — a detail that made his death land even harder. The night he died, the hashtag 'I want freedom of speech' briefly broke through censorship and trended nationally before being scrubbed, one of the fastest and most visible censor mobilizations of the Xi era.

events.label: The Wuhan Lockdown
events.description: On January 23, 2020, China sealed Wuhan — a city of eleven million, roughly the size of London — in a 76-day lockdown that became the blueprint for zero-COVID and the most-watched emergency public-health experiment in modern history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Xi Jinping later said he personally authorized the lockdown decision. The WHO, while noting it exceeded its own standard guidelines, publicly praised the move as a bold act of containment. At the time of the lockdown announcement, hundreds of thousands of residents had already left Wuhan for the Lunar New Year holiday, a timing that shaped the early international spread of the virus.

events.label: The Zero-COVID Policy
events.description: China's zero-COVID policy — mass testing, immediate snap lockdowns the moment any case appeared, mandatory quarantine camps, and contact-tracing apps tied to a person's right to enter buildings or board transit — aimed to drive the virus to zero in every outbreak and then resume normal life.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The strategy's internal logic was fundamentally different from the 'living with COVID' approach adopted by most democracies: it treated each outbreak as a discrete emergency to be extinguished rather than a chronic risk to be managed. For most of 2020 and 2021 it genuinely held deaths to a tiny fraction of Western tolls, which the government broadcast as evidence of systemic superiority — a claim that had real force before the policy's collapse.

events.label: The Shanghai Lockdown
events.description: In spring 2022, Shanghai — China's wealthiest, most internationally connected city — was locked down for roughly two months to contain an Omicron outbreak, confining twenty-five million people in conditions that shocked the country: food shortages, families forcibly separated, pets killed in buildings.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Shanghai was the city where the contradiction of zero-COVID became impossible to ignore: it was home to China's largest expatriate community, its biggest financial hub, and many of the country's most educated and internationally aware residents — the people least likely to accept the logic of indefinite confinement without complaint. Videos of residents shouting from balconies and drone footage of officials broadcasting lockdown instructions circulated globally and could not be fully suppressed domestically.

events.label: The White Paper Protests
events.description: After a fire in a locked-down apartment building in Urumqi, Xinjiang killed at least ten people — with witnesses saying lockdown barriers may have impeded escape — protesters in dozens of cities and elite universities took to the streets in November 2022, many holding up blank A4 sheets of white paper as a symbol of everything they were not permitted to say.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The protests were the widest open defiance since 1989, spanning Beijing, Shanghai, Chengdu, Wuhan, and campuses including Tsinghua, China's most prestigious university. The blank paper became one of the most striking protest symbols of the decade precisely because its meaning was self-evident and impossible to ban: the paper itself was the censorship. At the furthest edge of the protests, a small number of demonstrators explicitly called for Xi Jinping to step down — a demand essentially unvoiced in public in China since Tiananmen.

events.label: The Abrupt Reopening
events.description: In December 2022, just weeks after the white-paper protests, China abruptly dismantled zero-COVID with almost no public announcement and no preparatory vaccination campaign for the elderly, triggering a massive wave of infections across a population with almost no natural immunity and low booster rates.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Independent epidemiologists estimated the sudden reopening killed between one and two million people in a matter of months — a toll the official statistics, which recorded only tens of thousands of COVID deaths, did not reflect. The reversal was so fast and so unexplained that many Chinese citizens struggled to understand whether it had even happened: local officials who had been threatening lockdowns days earlier were suddenly silent. The mismatch between official and estimated death tolls became one of the most cited pieces of evidence for systematic Chinese data manipulation.

events.label: Xi's Third Term
events.description: The 20th Party Congress in October 2022 gave Xi Jinping a third five-year term as general secretary, shattering the two-term norm Deng Xiaoping had built to prevent a repeat of Mao, and filled the Politburo Standing Committee entirely with Xi loyalists.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The congress ended with a moment broadcast live around the world: former president Hu Jintao, frail and apparently confused, was firmly taken by the arm by an aide and led from the stage while Xi watched without reaction. The image was read internationally as a deliberate public humiliation of the collective-leadership era — though the Chinese government later said Hu had left for health reasons. The 2,296 delegates at the congress were chosen through a process ultimately controlled by Xi, meaning the body that confirmed his third term had itself been assembled to ensure that outcome.

events.label: The Property Crisis
events.description: The 2021 default of Evergrande (Héngdà in Mandarin), once the world's most indebted property developer, cracked the debt-fueled real-estate model that had powered roughly a quarter of China's entire economy since the 2008 stimulus — and no replacement engine has been identified.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Evergrande had liabilities exceeding $300 billion at the time of its default — the largest property-company debt load in history. The crisis was not just about one company: dozens of developers defaulted in the following years, millions of apartments that buyers had pre-purchased and paid for remained unfinished, and the property sector's contraction dragged government land-sale revenues (a major source of local government funding) down sharply. The combination of developer defaults, unfinished homes, and local government fiscal stress became the defining structural problem of the post-COVID Chinese economy.

events.label: Common Prosperity and the Tech Crackdown
events.description: A regulatory assault that scrapped Ant Group's IPO and humbled Alibaba, Didi, and the tutoring industry signaled the party reclaiming primacy over private capital.

events.label: The Population Turns Down
events.description: China's total population fell in 2022 for the first time since the Great Leap Forward famine of the early 1960s, beginning what demographers expect to be a long structural decline — decades earlier than the government's own projections had assumed.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: China was the world's most populous country until India surpassed it in the first half of 2023. The decline is the combined product of the one-child policy's long demographic echo, a sharp drop in births since the late 2010s, and a cultural shift among younger urban Chinese who increasingly choose not to marry or have children regardless of government incentives. The combination of a shrinking workforce, a rapidly aging population, and slowing economic growth raises the classic 'grow old before you grow rich' problem that China's planners have spent decades trying to avoid.

events.label: The Post-COVID Malaise
events.description: By mid-2023, China's official youth unemployment rate (for those aged 16–24) hit 21.3 percent before the government abruptly stopped publishing the monthly figure, a sign of the economic stagnation and confidence collapse that followed COVID's end.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The halt in publishing youth unemployment data was itself read as an admission of how politically sensitive the number had become. China's economy is still the second-largest in the world by nominal GDP and the largest by purchasing power parity, but the post-COVID years broke a forty-year assumption: that growth would always be fast enough to absorb discontent. The term 'lying flat' (tǎng píng) — opting out of competitive career-and-consumption culture — had gone viral in 2021 among young Chinese, and the youth unemployment crisis gave it material weight.

events.label: Toward 2049
events.description: With term limits gone and a 2049 centenary deadline written into official doctrine, Xi's China has staked its legitimacy on delivering 'national rejuvenation' — global power status, Taiwan 'reunification,' and technological leadership — in place of the growth-driven social contract that sustained the previous four decades.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The 2049 goal is paired with a 2035 interim target — 'basically realizing socialist modernization' — giving the regime a mid-century roadmap with two checkpoints. The bet is structurally different from the Deng-to-Hu era's implicit bargain ('we deliver growth, you stay out of politics'): as growth slows, nationalism and great-power status must carry more of the legitimacy load. Analysts call this the 'performance legitimacy' shift — moving from material delivery to identity and pride as the main reason the public accepts one-party rule.
